title: France's Bond Rout Breaks 24-Year Record as Riyadh Postpones Its Investment Showcase
subhead: French 10-year yields top 4.9%, the highest since 2002, as budget paralysis meets the worst street unrest in decades. Riyadh pulls its flagship FII conference, and Washington keeps Russian sanctions suspended while Iran talks grind on.

sections.heading: France pays 2002 prices for 2026 politics
sections.body:
French 10-year bond yields have topped 4.9%, up more than 130 basis points since June, putting borrowing costs at their highest level since 2002, according to Al Jazeera's markets explainer published today. National debt stands at roughly 3.6 trillion euros, or 119% of GDP - up from 98% in 2019 - and the deficit is projected at 5.4% of GDP in 2026 versus an EU average just above 3%.

The trigger is not the debt stock. It is the inability to legislate against it. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is trying to push through a budget with 54 billion euros in savings while Marine Le Pen of National Rally and Jean-Luc Melenchon of France Unbowed - the two leading candidates for the 2027 presidential race - both oppose the package. The government may have to invoke a constitutional clause to bypass parliament entirely.

INSEAD economist Antonio Fatas told Al Jazeera the numbers are not dramatically worse than peers: 'Are the French numbers much worse than other countries? No, but marginally they are worse, and the real difficulty here is that the political situation is such that the current government does not have an easy path to put together a budget that makes sense from a debt sustainability point of view.' Victor Lequillerier of Paris think tank BSI Economics added that debt sustainability 'depends far more on its trajectory, structure, and broader economic and financial context' than on the absolute level.

The move coincides with the worst social unrest in France in decades: school protests that began on September 21 in a poor Paris borough have spread nationwide, merging with public sector strikes against spending cuts, with roughly 1,800 arrests reported during weekend demonstrations.
sections.whyItMatters: France is now priced closer to a stressed sovereign than a core euro area borrower, and the spread to Germany has to absorb a political risk premium that no fiscal package can settle before the April 2027 election. That leaves the ECB carrying contagion risk it has no mandate to address directly.

sections.heading: Riyadh cancels Davos in the Desert, and the Gulf's capital-raising calendar slips
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia has postponed the Future Investment Initiative (FII) until 2027, cancelling an event that was due to run October 26-29. The FII Institute announced the decision on Tuesday, with CEO Maha Bint Mishari Al Saud framing it as a quality decision tied to the tenth edition. The stated rationale was scale and standards; the timing is Houthi strikes on Saudi cities.

The conference is the kingdom's main annual showcase for attracting foreign capital into its diversification programme, and the speaker list read like a roll call of Western finance: Ruth Porat of Alphabet, David Solomon of Goldman Sachs, and Laurence Fink of BlackRock were scheduled. The Houthis have struck military, energy and civilian infrastructure including Riyadh's international airport, killing at least 18 people.

The physical disruption is spreading through the capital's financial district. Government agencies in Riyadh have instructed staff to work from home Monday to Thursday, and the Kingdom Centre - which houses the IMF's regional office - asked workers to stay away until further notice, per AFP reporting cited by Al Jazeera. Firms in the King Abdullah Financial District, where major US companies keep offices, have done the same.
sections.whyItMatters: Losing the year's marquee Gulf capital-markets event is a real cost, not a scheduling inconvenience: PIF-linked dealmaking, fund commitments and IPO marketing runs through FII week. It also signals that Riyadh's pitch to foreign investors is now competing with a security story it cannot control.

sections.heading: Sanctions policy becomes a price-of-diesel instrument
sections.body:
President Trump signed an executive order on Friday suspending sanctions on Russia and on countries buying its oil and gas, days before restrictions were due to bite under the Graham Act - legislation the Senate passed 86-11 and Trump signed last month. The order cites the national interest and sets no date for implementation, leaving the measures suspended at executive discretion.

The backlash is bipartisan and unusually sharp. Republican Senator Thom Tillis called it 'beyond irresponsible' and asked: 'What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisers not understand?' Republican John Cornyn said the late Senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the bill, 'would be appalled'. Democrats Don Beyer and Elizabeth Warren accused the administration of betraying Ukraine and defying Congress. President Zelenskyy said easing pressure 'only encourages him to keep attacking'.

The law would have permitted tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries still buying Russian oil and gas or helping Moscow evade sanctions. The waiver followed a US deal to buy Russian diesel announced on October 9 to lower fuel prices that rose during the US-Israeli war on Iran. Congress is in recess until after the November 3 midterms, limiting immediate pushback; Representative Gregory Meeks has introduced a bill to block the separate diesel deal.
sections.whyItMatters: Secondary sanctions were the West's strongest financial weapon against Russian revenue. Trading them for fuel supply sets a precedent that sanctions architecture is elastic when domestic pump prices are at stake - and that any future threat of 100% secondary tariffs carries less credibility.

sections.heading: Iran talks: a seven-day proposal sits unanswered as Hormuz stays shut
sections.body:
Qatar's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said negotiations between Washington and Tehran are continuing, with mediators shuttling messages and regional partners involved. 'The fact that we're not hearing about it is a good sign that we're doing our job properly,' he said at the Global Security Forum in Doha.

The substance is on the table and stationary. Iran's seven-day proposal would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear negotiations in exchange for lifting the naval blockade on Iranian ports and easing economic sanctions. The US has not responded. Analyst Negar Mortazavi said the door is open but talks are stuck on terms and sequencing: 'Tehran wants to end the war, but it is not prepared to surrender under military or economic pressure.' Two tankers, each carrying about two million barrels of crude, caught fire after hitting mines in the strait on Sunday, with the IRGC saying they used an unauthorised route.

Separately, US Ambassador to Turkiye and Special Envoy for Syria Tom Barrack told the same forum that Washington is exiting the oil-for-security bargain: 'The bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We're not leaving.' He said the US had been involved in 23 regime changes across the wider Middle East and that 'every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake.'
sections.whyItMatters: The sequencing gap is the whole negotiation: Tehran wants sanctions relief and the blockade lifted before reopening the strait, Washington wants the waterway first. Every day that gap holds, the risk premium in energy and shipping stays embedded - and Barrack's remarks quietly lower expectations that regime change is a US objective worth paying for.

sections.heading: The IMF leaves Bangkok with a debt warning and two new programmes
sections.body:
As the IMF's annual meetings closed in Bangkok on Saturday, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said low-income countries now spend 8 to 14 percent of government revenue on debt repayments, up from prior years, with higher global rates and dollar funding costs driving the increase. Vulnerable economies are also missing the AI investment boom that is lifting richer markets.

Georgieva described the mood among policymakers as carrying 'optimism and worry' - resilience and AI dynamism on one side, inflation, debt, wars and climate risk on the other. She said the Fund has a responsibility to help restructure debt where needed and is pursuing 'more resources for low-income countries.'

Two programmes moved forward. Georgieva said the IMF will back Iraq 'very firmly' with a requested loan programme, delivering 'both money and policy support.' On Lebanon, she said talks are 'very intense' with 'significant progress towards the programme,' though more work remains. IMFC chairman and Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan warned in the committee statement that escalating conflicts could 'further disrupt critical trade routes' and worsen energy and food security.
sections.whyItMatters: Debt service at 14% of revenue is the level where governments cut capital spending and subsidies - the point where fiscal distress becomes political instability. Iraq and Lebanon are both war-adjacent economies where an IMF programme is now effectively a financial stabilisation instrument tied to the Iran conflict.

sections.heading: European rates are repricing at the long end
sections.body:
The French move is part of a broader long-end selloff. Al Jazeera's markets coverage notes that France's 130bp rise since June has pushed 10-year yields to 2002 levels, while the site's own energy reporting today cites 10-year Bund yields at their highest since 2009, with UBS's Justinus Steinhorst flagging the combination of sustained high oil and a widening term premium.

That leaves the ECB in an awkward position. Inflation pressure from energy is arguing against easing, while sovereign spreads in the bloc's second-largest economy are arguing for caution on any signal that could be read as complacency. The euro area has no explicit spread-control mandate outside the existing anti-fragmentation toolkit, and none of it is designed for a member state whose problem is parliamentary arithmetic rather than market access.
sections.whyItMatters: Long-end yields rising across core Europe while energy keeps inflation sticky narrows the ECB's room in both directions. If French spreads widen further, the question shifts from whether the ECB acts to what instrument it has that does not look like fiscal policy.

bottomLine: Today's story is that political risk is being repriced in bond markets rather than in equity or FX. France is paying 2002-level yields on 119% debt because its parliament cannot pass a budget, not because its fundamentals collapsed - a distinction the market is currently declining to make. Riyadh postponed its flagship investment conference as Houthi strikes force the capital's financial district to work from home, which is the first time this war has visibly cost the Gulf its ability to convene capital. Washington has suspended the Graham Act's 100% secondary tariffs indefinitely to keep diesel flowing, weakening the credibility of the sanctions threat while Iran's seven-day Hormuz proposal sits unanswered in Doha. The IMF closed its meetings warning that the poorest borrowers spend up to 14% of revenue on debt service, with new programmes for Iraq and Lebanon in the pipeline. Watch French spreads against Bunds, the ECB's long-end language, and whether Washington responds to Tehran's sequencing terms before shipping insurers reprice the strait again.
